prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: The, Sometimes, God

outputs.L1:
The redbreast kills and kills itself against the window.  
Sooner or later, the blood in the breast will break the window  
into hundreds of pieces you can swallow whole.

Keep swallowing.

The redbreast loves you and wants you to remember the love,  
so it makes you puke into the toilet, blind.

I was blinded by love  
and drowned in an empty bathtub,  
spitting up birdshit,  
covered in red feathers.

•  

Sometimes the redbreast likes anting with lit cigarettes,  
safety pins, paper cuts.

God, that feels good.

It wraps everything in pretty pink gauze,  
the color of fake sunset.

Look: it is a pink soul!

It wants to get naked,  
and it wants it to hurt.

Red teeth.  
Red toes.  
Open mouths.

Who keeps pressing my head into the sidewalk  
inside the bathroom?

Who keeps the lights on?  
The lights stay on.

Who dissolves on my tongue?  
Who flies from my finger?

•  

The redbreast sits inside,  
behind your left eye,  
behind your right,  
and cleans its babies with its beak.

Scrubs its babies clean.

Shakes its tail feathers to scour the floor  
behind your forehead,  
and scours the floor red.

My brain is a cutter.  
My initials are beats per second,  
scrubbed down to zero  
by the rubies in the halo.

I whispered your name into the red air,  
and you answered.
outputs.L2:
The redbreast keeps hurling itself at the glass, destroying itself there.  
Eventually, the blood in its chest will shatter the window into countless fragments small enough to gulp down.  
Go on swallowing.

The redbreast adores you and needs you to keep that devotion in mind,  
so it drives you, sightless, to vomit into the toilet.  
Love took away my vision.  
I sank in a dry bathtub, coughing up bird filth,  
my body buried in crimson feathers.

Sometimes the redbreast pleasures itself by pressing against burning cigarettes, safety pins, paper-sliced skin.  
God, it feels wonderful.  
It bandages everything in soft rose gauze, the shade of an artificial dusk.  
See—there is a pink spirit.  
It wants exposure, and it wants pain to come with it.

Scarlet teeth. Scarlet toes.  
Mouths hanging open.

Who is forcing my face down against the pavement inside the bathroom?  
Who leaves the lights burning? They never go out.  
Who melts across my tongue?  
Who takes flight from my hand?

The redbreast lives within you,  
behind one eye and then the other,  
using its beak to wash its young.  
It scrapes its babies spotless.  
It flicks its tail to scour the ground behind your brow,  
and the floor of the mind turns red.

My brain cuts itself.  
My initials pulse like beats each second,  
rubbed away to nothing  
by the jewels circling the halo.

I breathed your name into the crimson air,  
and you replied.
outputs.L3:
The redbreast in the poem symbolizes a destructive form of love, one that injures both itself and the speaker. Rather than representing tenderness, comfort, or natural beauty, the bird becomes an image of emotional violence. Its love is not gentle or healing; it is dangerous, compulsive, and self-damaging. By focusing on the redbreast’s wounded body and painful actions, the poem suggests that love can become a force that harms the lover as much as the beloved.

This connection between love and bodily harm appears throughout the poem. Love is associated with blindness, vomiting, drowning, and red feathers, creating a physical language of suffering. These images make emotion feel visceral and unavoidable, as though love is not only felt in the heart or mind but experienced as an injury to the whole body. The red feathers especially emphasize the link between beauty and violence: they are vivid and striking, but their redness also suggests blood, pain, and raw exposure.

The redbreast is also portrayed as actively seeking pain. Images such as lit cigarettes, safety pins, and paper cuts suggest small but sharp forms of injury, the kind of pain that is intimate, deliberate, and repeated. These details make the bird seem drawn to its own suffering, almost as if pain is part of how it understands love. The poem therefore presents desire as something that can become self-destructive, turning affection into a cycle of wounding.

For the speaker, this violence is not external only. It becomes invasive and internal, as if the redbreast has entered their eyes and mind. The bird’s presence inside the speaker suggests that destructive love has taken over their perception and thoughts. The speaker cannot simply observe the redbreast from a distance; they are inhabited by it. This creates a sense of psychological torment, where the boundaries between the self and the damaging object of love begin to collapse.

By the end of the poem, the speaker calls out into a red, painful atmosphere and receives an answer. This ending suggests that the speaker remains trapped within the world of the redbreast, surrounded by the same imagery of blood, injury, and desire that has shaped the poem throughout. The response they receive may imply connection, but it is not necessarily comforting. Instead, it reinforces the poem’s central idea: love, in this vision, is a form of contact that is inseparable from pain.
outputs.L4:
The text explores a form of love that is inseparable from self-destruction. Through surreal and violent imagery, the redbreast becomes a figure of wounded devotion: it repeatedly injures itself, yet its suffering is not presented as accidental or external, but as something bound to the very act of loving. The bird’s body is fragile, exposed, and repeatedly violated, suggesting that love in this world does not heal or protect. Instead, it opens the self to pain, making injury feel almost necessary.

As the redbreast enters and inhabits the speaker’s body, the boundary between lover and beloved begins to collapse. The bird is no longer simply an image outside the speaker; it becomes internal, living inside the speaker’s flesh and memory. This creates a disturbing intimacy, as if love requires possession, invasion, and bodily transformation. The speaker’s body becomes a site where affection, trauma, and remembrance are all stored together. Love is not only felt emotionally but experienced physically, as a wound that cannot be separated from the self.

The imagery also suggests psychic violation. The redbreast’s presence inside the speaker can be read as a memory that refuses to disappear, a painful attachment that continues to move and bleed within the mind. The repeated wounding of the bird mirrors the repetition of emotional suffering: the same hurt is returned to again and again, as though pain has become a ritual. In this sense, suffering becomes a form of devotion. To love is to remember, and to remember is to reopen the wound.

At the same time, the text does not romanticize this suffering entirely. The violence is excessive and unsettling, showing that love can become annihilating when it depends on injury for its meaning. The redbreast’s self-destruction reveals the danger of a love that consumes both body and spirit. What begins as devotion becomes a force of erasure, leaving the speaker haunted by an intimacy that is also invasive and destructive.

Ultimately, the text presents love as a paradox: it is both deeply intimate and profoundly damaging. The redbreast symbolizes the way love can live inside a person long after it has become painful, turning memory into a wound and devotion into a form of self-harm. Through its surreal bodily imagery, the text suggests that some forms of love do not simply hurt; they transform suffering into the very language through which love is expressed.
outputs.L5:
**The Sometimes God**

The Sometimes God is the quiet presence people notice in uncertain moments. Sometimes, God feels close in the warmth of a sunrise, the kindness of a stranger, or the peace that comes after a difficult day. Other times, God may seem distant, hidden behind silence, questions, or pain.

The idea of the Sometimes God reminds us that faith is not always constant or easy. It can change with our experiences, our emotions, and the challenges we face. Sometimes we believe strongly, and sometimes we doubt. Yet even in doubt, there can be meaning.

For many people, God is found not only in miracles or grand events, but in small, ordinary moments. The sound of rain, the comfort of friendship, or the courage to keep going can all feel like signs of something greater. Sometimes, God is not an answer, but a gentle reminder that we are not alone.

In this way, The Sometimes God is a symbol of hope, mystery, and patience. It teaches that faith can exist even when it is imperfect, and that sometimes, simply continuing to seek is enough.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an experimental prose poem in a visceral, surreal horror style centered on a “redbreast” bird as a symbol of self-destructive love, with fragmented spacing, violent imagery, and no explanatory commentary.
counterfactuals.output:
the redbreast returns  
through the window I never opened

a fist of feathers  
wet with dawn  
wet with my name

it beats itself against the mirror  
until the room learns blood

love,  
you said,  
is a small bird  
kept warm beneath the ribs

so I opened

so I became weather  
for its little red catastrophe

        tap  
                tap  
        tap

each strike a kiss  
each kiss a nail  
each nail flowering inward

the redbreast sings  
with a throat full of glass

and I answer  
by pulling the song deeper

down past the lungs  
past the black orchard of the heart  
where all my roots are teeth

I have fed it  
crumbs of sleep  
threads of skin  
the soft blue milk of my wrists

still it hungers

still it wears your eyes  
like two wet seeds

O little wound with wings  
O chapel of meat  
O bright-breasted omen  
trying to hatch inside my mouth

I loved you  
until the walls molted

I loved you  
until my hands became cages  
and my cages became mouths  
and my mouths begged  
to be bitten shut

the redbreast circles

inside the skull  
inside the lamp  
inside the red cup of my pulse

it builds a nest  
from apologies  
from hair  
from the torn lace of old promises

then sets the nest on fire

        I hold it anyway

        I hold it  
        while it burns

its beak opens  
and out spills summer  
rotting and sweet

maggots of sunlight  
crawl over the floor

your voice comes after them  
barefoot  
smiling  
carrying the knife by the blade

do you remember

how gently we ruined each other

the redbreast remembers

it pecks my chest  
as if knocking at a door

as if someone inside  
might still forgive it

as if love  
were not this red machinery  
chewing itself clean

        tap  
                tap  
                        tap

my sternum splits  
like overripe fruit

the bird enters

no—

the bird exits

no—

the bird is the wound  
making wings of me

and I am the sky  
learning to bleed downward

somewhere  
a garden unlocks its jaw

somewhere  
the roses clap  
with severed hands

somewhere  
you are saying stay

and the redbreast  
obedient to hunger  
throws itself again  
and again  
and again

against the heart’s last window

until love is only feathers

until feathers are only ash

until ash opens its red mouth

and sings
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a disturbing free-verse poem that blends romance, bodily harm, religious imagery, and a robin/redbreast crashing into a window; make it dense, hallucinatory, and punctuation-light.
counterfactuals.output:
your mouth was a chapel  
with the doors nailed open  

and I came to kneel there  
thorn drunk  
salt lit  
carrying my little bowl of bloodless prayers  

outside  
the robin struck the window  

a redbreast comet  
a soft sacrament  
beak first into the invisible law  

and the glass sang once  
like a saint being broken  

you touched my wrist  
where the pulse kept throwing itself  
against its narrow cage  
and called it devotion  

all evening the room filled with feathers  
though the bird lay still  
though the sky went on pretending  
it had not hurled a heart at us  

love  
you said  
is the bruise God leaves  
when He tries to enter gently  

so I let you trace the blue scripture  
under my skin  
let the candles bend their small necks  
let the saints in their painted wounds  
look down with their gold shocked eyes  

the robin opened inside my head  
again and again  
red sermon  
red lantern  
red fist of music  

and the window remained pure  
unapologetic  
a sheet of frozen heaven  

we kissed beneath it  
like witnesses at an execution  
like children licking honey  
from the blade of a miracle  

your hands were warm  
your hands were bells  
your hands were animals  
that knew the way to hurt  
and call it home  

somewhere the bird’s breast  
kept blooming  
a rose in reverse  
a tiny altar cloth darkening  
beneath the vast indifferent hymn  

and I loved you then  
with my whole damaged body  
with every cracked rib praising  
with every nerve genuflecting  

until dawn came pale and surgical  
and found us  
haloed in dust  
our shadows tangled on the floor  

the window bright  
the robin gone  

only one red feather left  
stuck to the glass  
like a kiss  
like a warning  
like the smallest possible crucifix

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a dark avant-garde poem about being blinded by love, using recurring red imagery, birds, bathrooms, blood, feathers, and intrusive thoughts, in one continuous block with strange line breaks.
counterfactuals.output:
I loved you until the room grew a red mouth  
and swallowed the mirror,  
until the bathroom tiles blinked back at me  
with little wet eyes,  
each grout-line a vein  
each faucet coughing rust like prophecy.  
Birds kept arriving inside my skull—  
cardinals, crows lacquered in sunset,  
a flamingo with a broken question for a neck—  
and all of them beat their wings against my thoughts  
until feathers clung to the sink,  
to the soap,  
to the pale moon of the toilet bowl  
where my reflection drowned  
in pieces.  
Love, you were a red cloth tied over my face,  
a velvet accident,  
a curtain soaked in theater-blood,  
and I walked through the house applauding walls,  
calling every bruise a door.  
The intrusive thoughts came tapping  
tap tap  
like beaks on porcelain,  
saying look,  
saying don’t look,  
saying the heart is just a bathroom  
where everyone goes to be alone  
and leaves something behind.  
I washed my hands  
and the water reddened,  
not with guilt, not exactly,  
but with the color of your name  
spreading its wings in the basin.  
Outside, birds circled the roof  
like dark commas  
in a sentence God refused to finish.  
Inside, I collected feathers from the drain,  
red feathers, black feathers,  
feathers soft as warnings,  
and pressed them to my eyelids  
until the world became warm static,  
until your silhouette burned through me  
like a stoplight in fog.  
I was blinded, yes—  
not by brightness  
but by repetition:  
red towel, red throat, red dawn,  
red thought nesting behind red thought,  
the mirror opening like a wound  
and singing your face back wrong.  
In the bathroom of my mind  
the birds never sleep.  
They perch on the shower rod,  
they sharpen their little deaths  
on the edge of the tub,  
they whisper your voice  
through mouthfuls of blood-bright feathers:  
love is a window painted shut,  
love is a flock flying inward,  
love is the blindfold that blushes  
when it lies.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: I want a raw surrealist poem in the style of contemporary trauma poetry: a redbreast inside the speaker’s body/head, love as sickness, self-harm metaphors, pink gauze, cigarettes, safety pins, and a final whispered name.
counterfactuals.output:
**redbreast**

there is a redbreast living in my skull  
not singing, exactly—  
more like coughing up dawn  
against the bone-white window  
of my forehead.

love came back with a thermometer  
under its tongue,  
said *open up,*  
said *this will only hurt  
because you are still holy somewhere.*

i let it in.

now my chest is a hospital room  
with no nurses,  
only pink gauze blooming from the vents,  
only cigarettes sleeping in a porcelain dish  
like small white ghosts  
who gave up breathing first.

the bird beats its red little sermon  
against my ribs.  
it wants out.  
i want out.  
we both pretend the body  
is not a locked drawer  
full of safety pins  
and old rain.

some nights i imagine my sadness  
as a seam i could unthread,  
a dress made of weather  
falling open at the throat.  
but the mirror keeps bandaging me  
with its terrible silver hands.

love, you fever.  
love, you rotten fruit in the mouth.  
love, you church bell rung underwater.  
i wore you like a wound  
and called it proof.

outside, the streetlights flicker  
their jaundiced halos.  
inside, the redbreast folds itself  
into the soft meat of my thinking  
and sleeps.

i press pink gauze to the moon.  
i pin my shadow back on.  
i smoke one last cigarette  
with the window closed.

then, into the dark,  
so softly even the bird must lean closer,  
i whisper—

*Mara.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a grotesque lyrical text about a redbreast that “loves you” but causes pain, vomiting, drowning, and mental collapse; use fragmented syntax, repetitions, and imagery of eyes, toilets, bathtubs, halos, and red feathers.
counterfactuals.output:
The redbreast loves you.  
It says so. It says so. It says so.

Red little throat like a wound with wings,  
red feathers stuck to the mirror,  
to the rim of the toilet,  
to your tongue.

It loves you into gagging.  
It loves you with its bright bead eyes—  
two wet pins,  
two black seeds planted in your skull.

You bend.  
You break.  
Porcelain halo, toilet halo,  
holy ring of bile and spit.

The redbreast sings: love you love you love you.  
A song like a finger down the throat.  
A song like bathwater climbing the walls.  
A song like all your thoughts  
turning soft  
turning white  
turning wrong.

In the bathtub, its reflection has too many eyes.  
In the bathtub, your hands are red feathers.  
In the bathtub, the water kisses your mouth shut.

It loves you under.  
It loves you lower.  
It loves you where the lungs forget  
what air was called.

Tiny claws on the rim.  
Tiny beak at the drain.  
Tiny halo made of rust and hair.

You hear it in the pipes:  
love you  
love you  
love you

and every word is a sickness.

Your head opens like a bathroom door.  
Inside: steam.  
Inside: eyes.  
Inside: a redbreast beating itself bloody  
against the light.

It loves you until the room tilts.  
Until the toilet blooms.  
Until the bathtub becomes a sky.  
Until your mind folds in half  
and half  
and half again.

Red feathers in your teeth.  
Red feathers in the water.  
Red feathers circling your face  
like saints,  
like flies,  
like little burning halos.

The redbreast loves you.  
It loves you so much it hurts.

It loves you so much  
you cannot keep it down.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
